      "narrative": "For first inversion major triads, Van Eps prescribes that the middle note may be deleted without spoiling the chordal result: 'The upper and lower notes of first inversion triads are major and minor sixth intervals apart. The sixth makes a very powerful two note chord and because of this power, the middle notes can be deleted without spoiling the chordal result.' (p.19, Chapter 2). The two-note sixth frame alone carries the harmonic identity.",

      "narrative": "Van Eps defines first inversion with explicit voice placement: 'In the 1st inversion the tonic is on top... in the 2nd inversion the tonic is second... in the root voicing the tonic is the lowest note.' (p.23, Chapter 2). The student must track tonic position across all three inversions as the primary organizational principle.",

      "narrative": "When working with sixth intervals derived from triads, Van Eps prescribes: 'When working with sixths it is very important to identify the related first or second inversion triad.' (p.115, Chapter 5). Every sixth double-stop must be mentally anchored to its parent triad inversion.",

      "function_role": "first-inversion-sixth-inference",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes that the first inversion triad is harmonically present even when the middle voice is absent: 'A first inversion triad is inferred with the middle note deleted in the first half of each station, and a root position triad is present in arpeggio form in the middle to last half of each station.' (p.115, Chapter 5). The student should treat the suggested tone as harmonically real.",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "super-position-voice-raising",
      "narrative": "For any major triad inversion, Van Eps prescribes the super/sub voice-movement system: 'When any one of the voices in a triad is raised one step of the scale it is placed in super position. When it is lowered one step of the scale it is placed in sub position.' (p.160, Chapter 8). The named inversion is the origin; raising the middle voice of a first inversion major triad automatically produces a second inversion member.",

      "function_role": "super-sub-origin-tracking",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes keeping the named inversion mentally active at all times during super/sub work: 'When working with the super and sub principle it is necessary to keep the named inversion in mind at all times because it is the origin; it is the original voicing that is going to produce others.' (p.160, Chapter 8). Losing the origin causes harmonic disorientation.",

      "function_role": "super-sub-as-chord-center-generation",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes treating every triad inversion as a generative center: 'SUPER AND SUB CONCEPT - All chords are centers - When voices in a chord are moved one step up or down in any scale the resulting change becomes another center.' (p.161, Chapter 8). Moving voices of a major triad by diatonic step produces new harmonic centers rather than mere embellishments.",

      "narrative": "Van Eps draws an explicit equivalence for first inversion major triads: 'First inversion triads with the upper voice motion sub are the exact same notation as root triads with the upper voice motion super.' (p.175, Chapter 9). The student should exploit this identity to navigate between inversion families without shifting position.",

      "function_role": "root-position-wide-reach-inclusion",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes including all root position voicings regardless of reach difficulty: 'In root triads most of the reaches are quite great. However, these voicings must be included no matter how impractical they may appear, because by design they belong to the family of basic triads.' (p.239, Chapter 10). No inversion may be omitted for convenience.",

      "function_role": "compromise-fingering-detached-voice",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes that when the sustained notation cannot be fully fretted, compromise fingerings are acceptable only when the moving voice is detached: 'The difference between an original notation and a compromise fingering is noticeable harmonically when the tones are sustained, but when the moving voice is detached and sounded separately there is no notation difference.' (p.239, Chapter 10).",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "two-voice-motion-half-note-sustain",
      "narrative": "When two voices move over a sustained third in a major triad context, Van Eps prescribes sustaining the half note full value, but permits releasing it if the reach is too great: 'If at first some of the reaches are too great, it is permissible to treat the half note as though it were a quarter note--to let go of the half note after sounding the triad. However, endeavor to sustain the half note full value.' (p.249, Chapter 11).",

      "function_role": "blockout-repeat-order-inversion-cycling",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes cycling all three major triad inversions in a fixed repeat order over an independent bass in blockout studies: 'When the three triad inversions are placed in a fixed uniform group that appears in exactly the same order over and over again, forming a pattern each measure or so thru the cycle, it is quite naturally termed a repeat order.' (p.290, Chapter 14). This systematizes voice-leading across the cycle of fifths.",

      "function_role": "bass-as-independent-fourth-voice",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes treating the bass line as entirely separate from the triad: 'Always think of the triad and bass as being separate isolated lines in an overall four note harmonic group of tones.' (p.273, Chapter 13). The major triad is a three-voice unit; the bass is a fourth independent voice that may contradict or color the triad's harmonic identity.",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "cycle-of-fifths-key-traversal",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes practicing all triad inversion studies through the descending cycle of fifths rather than chromatically: 'Most of the studies in these books go through the keys employing the descending cycle of fifths (up a fourth or down a fifth) in preference to changing keys chromatically.' (p.18, Chapter 2). This is the master organizational principle for all inversion drilling.",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "tone-suggestion-harmonic-economy",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes using implied tones to reduce voicing density while preserving harmonic identity: 'A very useful tool in harmonic voicing (for all instruments) is: the hint/suggestion of a tone. A note can be inferred but not actually sounded, yet its presence is felt to the point where it is almost heard.' (p.20, Chapter 2). Major triad voicings may omit inner voices when the outer frame and overtones supply the missing information.",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "delayed-coupling-extended-voicing",
      "narrative": "When a major triad contains more notes than can be sounded simultaneously, Van Eps prescribes arpeggiating with delayed coupling: 'Another effective method to Experiment with in the illusionary art of compounding triads or any chords that contain more notes than can be sounded Simultaneously is by a delayed type of coupling--The ear will remember the first notes sounded and automatically couple them to the next notes thus forming an overall harmonic picture.' (p.21, Chapter 2).",

      "chord_quality": "major-triad",
      "function_role": "moving-inner-voice-space-requirement",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes giving inner voices room to be heard within a major triad texture: 'Moving lines must have space. In order for an inner voice to be able to stand out in any harmonic situation it must be given room to be heard.' (p.17, Chapter 1). Voice density must be managed so that moving lines are not masked by sustained outer voices.",

      "chord_quality": "minor-triad",
      "function_role": "melodic-minor-up-harmonic-minor-down-voicing",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes a specific scale assignment per voice when voicing minor triads through inversions: 'Triads - 1st - 2nd And Root - Melodic minor up, middle voice - harmonic minor down, lower voice.'       "chord_quality": "minor-triad",
      "function_role": "minor-mode-cannot-parallel-major",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes recognizing that minor mode inversion patterns cannot be directly mapped from major: 'The Minor Modes Can't Parallel the Major because of the Minor third interval--it is shortened by one semitone.' (p.159, Chapter 7). Minor triad inversions require independent study; the major inversion shapes do not transfer.",

      "chord_quality": "minor-triad",
      "function_role": "blockout-root-first-second-inversion-all-used",
      "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes employing all three minor triad inversions in blockout studies alongside major inversions: 'Triads, both major and minor are employed in the following blockouts; root, first and second inversions are used.'       "chord_quality": "minor-triad",
      "function_role": "super-sub-applied-to-minor",
      "narrative": "The super/sub principle applies equally to minor triads: Van Eps states 'Place in all keys - Major and both Minors - sustain the middle voice - reverse the direction of voice motion = open to closed.' (p.253, Chapter 11). Minor triad inversions must be drilled with the same super and sub voice movements as major triads, in both melodic and harmonic minor.",

      "function_role": "bass-independence-minor-triad-four-voice",
      "narrative": "As with major triads, Van Eps prescribes treating the bass as a fourth independent voice beneath minor triads: 'The bass lines are completely independent of the triads.       "chord_quality": "minor-triad",
      "function_role": "do-not-depress-unused-strings",
      "narrative": "Van Eps's fatigue-factor rule applies equally to minor triad voicings: 'Don't depress more strings than are being used because of the fatigue factor.' (p.8, Chapter 1). For minor triad inversions with wide string-set skips, only the active strings should be fretted.",

      "function_role": "nontraditional-configurations-must-be-sought",
      "narrative": "Van Eps's prescription to explore nontraditional configurations applies to minor triads as well: 'Traditional configurations are well known; nontraditional configurations must be found, explored, analyzed, and well practiced.'       "narrative": "Van Eps prescribes using chromatic exercises through all four triad qualities as a scale-construction tool: 'By using these chromatic exercises in all their various forms, positions, and combinations, all scales Maj., Min., Dim., Aug. may be constructed.'
